title: Addition vs Multiplication
coreInsight: Disjoint alternatives combine by addition, while sequential choices combine by multiplication when each branch's continuations are counted correctly.
targetLearnerRealization: Disjoint alternatives combine by addition, while sequential choices combine by multiplication because each first choice branches into later choices.
learningObjectives: Distinguish separate alternatives from stages that every final outcome must complete.
Explain multiplication using 'for each first choice' language and a complete outcome grid.
Check disjointness and branch sizes before adding or multiplying counts.

continuity.openingCallback: Use F1's reasonableness habit to estimate the size of a small choice space before counting it exactly.
closingSeeds: When branches have different lengths or later choices depend on earlier ones, a systematic list or tree can keep every outcome visible.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: The words 'or' and 'and' mechanically determine addition or multiplication in every problem.
Every branch is assumed to have the same number of continuations.
Overlapping alternatives can be added without correction.
Counting steps and counting final outcomes are the same thing.

beats.purpose: Reactivate F1's reasonableness habit without pre-solving the exact count.
beats.expectedRealization: Two small choice lists create a small collection of outfits, so an exact result near 5 is reasonable and one near 50 is not.
beats.transitionIn: In F1, you used size and structure to predict what an answer should feel like. Keep that habit for a new kind of question.
beats.prompt: A closet has 2 shirts and 3 pairs of pants. One outfit uses one shirt and one pair of pants. Before counting exactly, should the number of outfits be closer to 5 or to 50?

feedback.near-five: Yes. Two short lists should create a single-digit number of pairs.
feedback.near-fifty: Fifty would require far more possibilities than these two short lists can supply.

beats.correctFeedback: Good estimate. Now make the exact outcomes visible.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compare the two short lists with the proposed sizes; 50 is much too large.

steps.body: An estimate does not give the exact count, but it sets a useful scale: expect only a handful of outfits.

resolution.takeaway: Predict the scale first; then build a count you can check against it.

beats.purpose: Let the learner construct the product count from all shirt-pants pairs before naming the multiplication principle.
beats.expectedRealization: Each of the two shirts continues to all three pants choices, creating six final outfits.
beats.transitionIn: The estimate says 'a handful.' Now count final outfits rather than the five objects in the closet.
beats.prompt: How many different outfits can be made?

visual.ariaLabel: Two shirt choices and three pants choices, not yet paired

response.feedback: Count complete shirt-pants pairs, not the separate clothing items.

beats.incorrectFeedback: For each shirt, pair it once with every pair of pants.

visual.ariaLabel: A two by three grid showing all six shirt and pants outfits

steps.title: Finish each outfit
steps.body: Blue continues to all 3 pants choices, and Gold also continues to all 3.

steps.title: Count the grid
steps.body: The grid has 2 rows with 3 complete outfits in each row.

steps.title: Another way
steps.body: The same two equal rows can be counted by repeated addition.

resolution.takeaway: Multiplication counts complete combinations: for each of 2 shirts, there are 3 pants choices.

beats.purpose: Extract the branching reason for multiplication rather than treating it as a keyword rule.
beats.expectedRealization: Multiplication works because every first choice has a complete set of later continuations.
beats.transitionIn: The six cells are not six clothing items; each cell records one finished path through both choices.

visual.ariaLabel: The completed two by three outfit grid

options.text: There are 2 shirts plus 3 pants, so multiply those objects.
For each of 2 shirts, all 3 pants choices complete an outfit.
There are 2 decision steps, so multiply by 2.

feedback.objects: The objects alone total 5; multiplication counts their complete pairings.
feedback.continuations: Exactly. Every row has the full set of three continuations.
feedback.steps: The number of steps does not tell how many choices occur at each step.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—'for each' describes the branching structure.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Point to one shirt row and ask how many complete outfits it contains.

steps.body: The first choice creates 2 branches. Each branch has 3 endings, so the final outcomes—not the decision steps—total 2 × 3.

resolution.takeaway: Multiply when every final outcome completes successive choices and the branch counts are known.

beats.purpose: Contrast a product of stages with a union of genuinely separate alternatives.
beats.expectedRealization: Choosing one dessert from either disjoint shelf gives two cases whose counts add.
beats.transitionIn: Now remove the second stage. You will choose one finished item from one shelf or the other.
beats.prompt: A cafe offers 2 cakes and 3 pies. You choose exactly one dessert. How many choices are there?

visual.ariaLabel: Two cake choices and three separate pie choices

response.feedback: A final choice is one displayed dessert, not a cake-pie pair.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—2 cake choices plus 3 pie choices makes 5 desserts.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Do you take one dessert, or one item from each shelf?

visual.ariaLabel: Five desserts separated into a two-item cake case and a three-item pie case

steps.title: Separate the cases
steps.body: Every allowed choice is either one cake or one pie.

steps.title: Check the split
steps.body: The two cases cover every dessert, and no dessert appears in both cases.

steps.title: Join the counts
steps.body: Add the sizes of the two disjoint cases.

resolution.takeaway: Add separate alternatives when they cover all outcomes without overlap.

beats.purpose: Name the addition and multiplication principles only after both structures have been experienced.
beats.expectedRealization: Addition joins disjoint finished alternatives; multiplication follows successive choices to finished outcomes.
beats.transitionIn: You have now used two different structures: separate shelves and a grid of completed pairs.
beats.name: Addition and multiplication principles
beats.conciseDefinition: Add counts for separate, non-overlapping alternatives. Multiply choice counts across stages that every final outcome completes.
beats.formalization: disjoint cases: a + b    |    successive choices: a × b
beats.memoryHook: Separate cases add; complete branches multiply.

beats.purpose: Break mechanical and/or keyword matching by classifying the outcome structure instead.
beats.expectedRealization: The operation follows whether outcomes come from separate cases or completed stages, not a particular word.
beats.transitionIn: The words can mislead. Sort by what one finished outcome contains.
beats.prompt: Sort each situation by its counting structure.

items.text: A shelf holds 4 comics and 3 atlases; choose one book.
Choose one starter from 2 choices or one dessert from 3 choices—not both.
Choose a route, then one departure time for that route.
Build an outfit by choosing a shirt, followed by pants.

response.feedback: Ask whether one outcome belongs to one case, or travels through every stage.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. The structure—not the presence of 'and' or 'or'—chooses the operation.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Ignore the linking words. Describe what one finished outcome contains.

cases.label: Join separate alternatives
items: Choose one book from the combined shelves
Choose either one starter or one dessert

visual.ariaLabel: The four situations correctly grouped by separate alternatives or successive stages

steps.body: The book sentence uses the word 'and,' yet one final choice is still a comic or an atlas, so the shelf counts add.
The route sentence never says 'and,' yet every trip needs both a route choice and a time choice.

resolution.takeaway: Decide what a complete outcome is before choosing an operation.

beats.purpose: Repair the assumption that every first choice automatically has the same number of continuations.
beats.expectedRealization: Nonuniform branches must be counted by their actual endings, here 2 + 3 rather than 2 × 3.
beats.transitionIn: Multiplication made the outfit grid quick because both shirt rows had the same length. What if the rows do not match?
beats.prompt: Blue Route has 2 departure times and Gold Route has 3. How many complete route-and-time trip plans are shown?

visual.ariaLabel: A route tree with two Blue Route endings and three Gold Route endings

response.feedback: Count the endpoints of the complete paths.

beats.incorrectFeedback: The two first branches do not have equal lengths; count 2 endings and 3 endings.

visual.ariaLabel: Five trip plans split into two Blue Route plans and three Gold Route plans

steps.title: Count actual continuations
steps.body: The Blue branch has 2 endpoints; the Gold branch has 3.

steps.title: Join the route cases
steps.body: A trip uses exactly one route, so these cases are disjoint.

resolution.takeaway: Multiply by a common branch size only when that size really applies to each first choice.

beats.purpose: Make overlap visible and require a distinct-outcome count before addition is trusted.
beats.expectedRealization: Adding case sizes double-counts any outcome appearing in both alternatives.
beats.transitionIn: Unequal cases can still be added. But addition has one more condition: the cases must not share outcomes.
beats.prompt: Chess members are Ana, Ben, and Chen. Music members are Ben and Dia. How many different students belong to at least one club?

visual.ariaLabel: Chess and music member lists, with Ben appearing on both lists

response.feedback: Count distinct students, not appearances on the two lists.

beats.incorrectFeedback: Ben appears twice on the lists but is only one student.

visual.ariaLabel: Four distinct students separated into chess only, both clubs, and music only

steps.title: Spot the repeat
steps.body: The raw list count 3 + 2 includes Ben twice.

steps.title: Count each student once
steps.body: Ana, Ben, Chen, and Dia are the four distinct outcomes.

resolution.takeaway: Before adding cases, check that they do not overlap—or correct the repeated count.

beats.purpose: Apply the primary multiplication structure in a fresh context with a complete worked visual resolution.
beats.expectedRealization: A finished signal contains both a light and a sound, so each light branches to all four sounds.
beats.transitionIn: Now use the full test on a fresh object: first define one finished outcome, then follow its stages.
beats.transitionOut: The signal count worked for the same reason as the outfit grid: every first choice had a complete set of continuations.
beats.whyNow: The learner has discovered and named both principles and can now justify a clean product without relying on clothing vocabulary.
beats.entryBridge: Treat one light-and-sound pair as one completed signal.
beats.exitBridge: Three light branches with four sound endings each create twelve completed signals.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The outfit grid becomes a light-by-sound outcome grid.
learnerPrompts: What choices must every finished signal contain?
How many sound continuations belong to each light choice?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Build one row for each light color and place all four sounds in every row.

visual.ariaLabel: A three by four grid of all light and sound signals

steps.title: Define one outcome
steps.body: A finished signal contains one light color and one sound.

steps.title: Count every branch
steps.body: For each of 3 light colors, any of the 4 sounds can follow.

resolution.takeaway: Successive choices multiply when every first choice has the counted later choices.

beats.purpose: Check independent recognition of disjoint alternatives in a low-context setting.
beats.expectedRealization: One selected item comes from exactly one of two non-overlapping shelves, so the counts add.
beats.transitionIn: First, isolate the separate-alternatives structure without a second decision stage.
beats.transitionOut: The two shelves formed complete, non-overlapping cases.
beats.whyNow: This gives clean independent evidence for the addition principle before structures are mixed.
beats.entryBridge: Ask whether one final choice uses one shelf or both shelves.
beats.exitBridge: Four comics and five puzzle books give nine one-book choices.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Two disjoint shelves like the earlier dessert cases.
learnerPrompts: Does one selection combine books from both shelves?
Can any book occur in both cases?
beats.incorrectFeedback: One selected book is either a comic or a puzzle book, never a pair.

visual.ariaLabel: Nine book choices separated into four comics and five puzzle books

steps.body: The 4 comic choices and 5 puzzle-book choices are separate and cover every allowed selection.

beats.purpose: Check independent use of the multiplication principle with two uniform stages.
beats.expectedRealization: Each cone uses both a flavor and a topping, producing a rectangular choice space.
beats.transitionIn: Now switch from one-of-two shelves to an object completed in two stages.
beats.transitionOut: Four flavor branches with three endings each create twelve cones.
beats.whyNow: The nearby context checks that the learner counts final pairs rather than adding available ingredients.
beats.entryBridge: Define one finished cone as a flavor-topping pair.
beats.exitBridge: The complete grid has four rows of three cones.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A rectangular outcome grid with one stage on each axis.
learnerPrompts: What two choices appear in every finished cone?
How many topping continuations does each flavor have?
beats.incorrectFeedback: For each of the 4 flavors, count all 3 topping choices.

visual.ariaLabel: A four by three grid of all flavor and topping cones

steps.body: Every flavor can be paired with every topping, so each of 4 flavor branches has 3 endings.

resolution.takeaway: Count finished combinations, not decision steps or ingredient objects.

beats.purpose: Check that the learner counts nonuniform continuations rather than multiplying arbitrary list sizes.
beats.expectedRealization: The two ferry cases have different numbers of endings, so their actual plan counts add to five.
beats.transitionIn: Uniform rows made multiplication compact. This schedule has rows of different lengths.
beats.transitionOut: Counting the actual endpoints handled the unequal branches safely.
beats.whyNow: This directly tests the mapped misconception that all first choices are assumed to have equal continuations.
beats.entryBridge: Separate the Harbor ferry plans from the Bay ferry plans, then count their endpoints.
beats.exitBridge: Three Harbor departures and two Bay departures make five distinct ferry-and-time plans.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The unequal route tree with one complete path per plan.
learnerPrompts: How many endings belong to each ferry branch?
Why is 2 × 3 not the branch structure here?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Count 3 endpoints under Harbor and 2 under Bay; the branch lengths differ.

visual.ariaLabel: Five complete ferry and departure-time paths

steps.body: Harbor produces 3 complete plans and Bay produces 2. A trip uses exactly one ferry, so the cases are disjoint.

resolution.takeaway: When branch lengths differ, count the endings each branch really has.

beats.purpose: Check nested use of addition within one stage followed by multiplication across stages.
beats.expectedRealization: The first stage has five disjoint symbol choices, and every symbol pairs with either border.
beats.transitionIn: Now one stage contains its own 'either' choice, but the finished tile still requires a second stage.
beats.transitionOut: Addition counted the choices inside the symbol stage; multiplication connected that stage to the border stage.
beats.whyNow: The composition makes keyword matching fail while keeping the arithmetic accessible.
beats.entryBridge: Count the available symbols first, then ask how many borders complete each symbol choice.
beats.exitBridge: Five symbol choices, each with two border choices, produce ten tiles.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Disjoint cases feeding a uniform second-stage grid.
learnerPrompts: How many choices are available in the symbol stage?
What later choice does every symbol receive?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—10 different tiles can be made.
beats.incorrectFeedback: First combine the 3 letter and 2 digit alternatives, then pair each symbol with 2 borders.

visual.ariaLabel: A five by two grid of all symbol and border tiles

steps.title: Count one stage
steps.body: The letter and digit lists are disjoint symbol alternatives.

steps.title: Complete every tile
steps.body: Each of the 5 symbols can receive either of 2 borders.

resolution.takeaway: Operations can nest: use the structure at each level, not one keyword for the entire problem.

beats.purpose: Synthesize products within disjoint cases and addition across them.
beats.expectedRealization: Count complete morning events and complete afternoon events separately, then add the disjoint time blocks.
beats.transitionIn: For a final challenge, each separate case now contains two stages of its own.
beats.transitionOut: The calculation mirrors the structure: multiply inside each branch, then add the branches.
beats.whyNow: This requires the learner to compose both C1 principles and justify coverage and non-overlap.
beats.entryBridge: Treat morning and afternoon as separate cases; inside each, complete the activity-room pair.
beats.exitBridge: Six morning events and six afternoon events combine to twelve one-event choices.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Two disjoint branches, each containing its own rectangular choice grid.
learnerPrompts: How many complete events are in each time block?
Why can the two block totals be added without overlap?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Multiply activity by room inside each time block, then add the non-overlapping blocks.

visual.ariaLabel: Six morning event combinations and six separate afternoon event combinations

steps.title: Morning branch
steps.body: Each of 2 workshops can use any of 3 rooms.

steps.title: Afternoon branch
steps.body: Each of 3 talks can use either of 2 rooms.

steps.title: Join disjoint branches
steps.body: One chosen event is morning or afternoon, never both.

resolution.takeaway: Multiply along complete branches; add across disjoint branches.

beats.purpose: Consolidate the structural tests for addition and multiplication before introducing the next lesson's tension.
beats.expectedRealization: Reliable counting requires defining final outcomes, checking disjoint coverage, and verifying continuations.
beats.transitionIn: Before opening a more complicated tree, collect the checks that made every count trustworthy.
beats.prompt: Which checks belong in a reliable addition-or-multiplication decision? Select all three.

options.text: Before adding cases, check that they cover everything without overlap.
Before multiplying, check how many continuations each branch really has.
Let the words 'and' and 'or' choose the operation automatically.

response.feedback: Use the structure of complete outcomes, not a keyword shortcut.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Those three checks distinguish trustworthy counts from guesses.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep the checks about outcomes, coverage, overlap, and real branch lengths.

visual.ariaLabel: Three checks for choosing and justifying a counting operation

resolution.takeaway: Add disjoint alternatives. Multiply successive choices when the branch counts justify it.

beats.purpose: Create the need for C2's systematic lists and trees only after consolidating C1.
beats.expectedRealization: When later choices vary with earlier ones, a visible organization is needed to count all endpoints exactly once.
beats.transitionIn: You can now handle a small uneven tree by counting its endpoints. Let the dependencies become more tangled.
beats.prompt: Suppose each route allows different stops, and each stop unlocks a different set of activities. How could you organize every complete plan so none is missed or repeated?
beats.takeaway: A single product may no longer describe the whole tree. Next, we will build systematic lists and trees that keep every path visible.

notes: Draft foundation lesson authored with the repo-local mathinking-lesson Skill.
The generated outfit-style investigation is used for discovery because it isolates the addition-versus-multiplication distinction.

The mapped bank ID resolves to an equal-cross-sums problem while its approved rationale describes license plates; the unrelated bank item is therefore not integrated and the approved mapping is unchanged.
All visuals use existing generic primitives; no lesson-specific renderer behavior was added.
